cards.text: The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, is writing down what he sees under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:1). Now he looks at the place of judgment and the place of righteousness, the spots where things are supposed to be set right.

cards.question: In the place of judgment and the place of righteousness, what does the Teacher find?

cards.text: That's like calling the fire department and finding out the fire department is the thing on fire. Then the Teacher says something in his heart about God.

cards.question: The Teacher says in his heart that God will judge both the righteous and the wicked.
The Teacher says God will judge the righteous and the wicked, since there is a ___ for every activity and every deed.

cards.text: Then the Teacher says something to himself about the sons of men. God tests them, he says, so they can see for themselves what they really are.

cards.question: What does the Teacher say God's test shows the sons of men they are?

cards.text: OUCH. Friend, I'm a cookie stamper with a mustache for hands, and even I felt that one. Then the Teacher looks at how men and animals die.

cards.question: How does the Teacher say men and beasts compare when they die?
The Teacher says men and beasts each have a different breath.

cards.text: Man has no advantage over the animals, the Teacher says, since everything is futile. I spent YEARS in a junk drawer feeling fancier than the rubber bands in there with me, and friend, we were in the SAME drawer.

cards.question: All go to one place: all come from dust, and all return to ___.

cards.text: Then the Teacher goes somewhere BIG, friend, the kind of thing I used to lie awake thinking about in that junk drawer. The spirit of man rising upward, and the spirit of the animal going down into the earth.

cards.question: The Teacher says he knows for sure that the spirit of man rises upward.

cards.text: And then, real quiet, the Teacher says he's seen what's best for a man.

cards.question: What does the Teacher say there's nothing better for a man than?
The Teacher says enjoying his work is a man's lot. What does he say nobody can bring a man to see?

cards.text: Then the Teacher looks again, and this time he considers all the oppression taking place under the sun. He sees the tears of the oppressed.

cards.question: The oppressed are in tears. What does the Teacher say they don't have?
The oppressed have no comforter, and the Teacher sees that the ___ lay in the hands of their oppressors.

cards.text: And there it is again: no comforter. So the Teacher weighs the dead against the living.

cards.question: The Teacher says he admired the living above the dead.

cards.text: I've had some dark years under the takeout menus in a junk drawer, friend, and even I need a minute with that one. But the Teacher's not done, because he names someone better off than both.

cards.question: Who does the Teacher say is better off than both the dead and the living?

answers.text: Someone who has not yet existed

cards.question: The one who has not yet existed is better off because he hasn't seen the ___ that is done under the sun.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to supply the exact word 'time' in 'there is a ___ for every activity and every deed.' No earlier card sets this up. The 'a time for every activity' idea comes from Ecclesiastes 3:1-8, which isn't part of this lesson and isn't told on any card. A baker who has only seen these cards has to guess the wording rather than reason it out, and 'law' could also fit the sentence.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Ecclesiastes 3:21 is a question: 'Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?' The card drops the 'who knows if' framing. It tells the verse as a plain picture ('The spirit of man rising upward, and the spirit of the animal going down into the earth'), which a baker can read as something the Teacher states. The card should tell it as the open question the text asks, without giving away card 14.

The wrong answer 'work' makes a sentence a baker could argue is right. Someone who has never existed also hasn't seen 'the work that is done under the sun,' and Ecclesiastes uses that exact phrase as something grievous (Ecclesiastes 2:17). This wrong answer should be replaced with one that can't be argued.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.
